newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Italy readies mini-budget to ensure EMU entry.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Italy readies mini-budget to ensure EMU entry.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi said on Wednesday he had prepared the framework for a fresh budget to ensure Italy is a founder member of the single European currency and would be launching the package in the coming weeks.

However the hard left Communist Refoundation, which secures Prodi's majority in the lower house of parliament, questioned whether fresh budgetary pain was worth the cost and cast doubt on the prospects for European economic and monetary union (EMU).

Just two months after launching an enormous 62.5 trillion lire ($37 billion) budget for 1997, Prodi's office said in a statement that Italy needed yet more action to tame the public sector deficit and meet tough criteria for EMU membership.
Financial markets expect a 14-15 trillion lire mini-budget.
Prodi said a new package of measures would be launched in the coming weeks as soon as the Treasury knew how much money had to be raised. Official state accounts are due in March.
"This budget, tied to progress already made, will allow Italy to meet the necessary objectives needed to fully satisfy the Maastricht Treaty," the statement said.
Prodi has visited Germany twice in the last two weeks to convince the EU's largest state of Italy's EMU credentials.

He now faces a battle to persuade Communist Refoundation, which has become the first major political force in Europe-friendly Italy to question the future of EMU, of the need for fresh belt-tightening.

"To prepare a mini-budget...for something which no-one believes in any more would be an expression of integrationalist stupidity," Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti said in an interview with La Repubblica newspaper.
"I know I'm not the only one to think that...Europe as laid out in the Maastricht treaty won't happen," he added.
In a statement released after Prodi had announced he would forge ahead with a mini-budget, Bertinotti said he was ready to discuss a possible package.
"As ever, the decisive word is contents...Communist Refoundation will not accept cuts in public spending or new taxes," he said.

Prodi said the new budget would be based on structural measures to enable Italy to adhere to the stability pact, agreed last year by European Union leaders, which establishes strict economic guidelines for eventual EMU partners.
Economists have pressed for cuts to Italy's bloated pensions system, but Refoundation has threatened to bring down Prodi's centre-left government if welfare spending is touched.
Italy has pledged to reduce its deficit to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997 to meet an important requirement of the Maastricht treaty.
The closely watched ratio ballooned to around seven percent last year after the deficit rocketed to 138.5 trillion lire against a revised target of 123 trillion.
To ram the figure lower, the government introduced a package of fresh taxes and spending cuts in its 1997 budget.
Analysts have warned that there is little scope for fresh fiscal action at a time when the economy is already struggling. ($1=1,684 lire)
